```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(epidemiologysuite)
```

Sample sizes for studies of a test's accuracy: estimating its sensitivity and specificity, showing it is better than a reference,
comparing two tests, and the area under the ROC curve. The numbers are computed when this page is built; the examples are those the
package's tests check against the published answers (`tests/testthat/test-calc_diagnostic.R`, `test-calc_roc.R`). Most come from
Akoglu, *User's guide to sample size estimation in diagnostic accuracy studies*, Turk J Emerg Med 2022;22(4):177-185. In the app:
**Plan: Sample Size > Diagnostic & Screening**.

## The prevalence decides the number

Sensitivity is estimated in the people **with** the condition and specificity in those **without** it. When the study enrols
consecutive patients, the number needed is the number of diseased (or non-diseased) people required, divided by the prevalence (or
by 1 minus the prevalence). A rare condition therefore makes sensitivity expensive.

## Estimating sensitivity and specificity

Akoglu's example (Table 3B): an expected sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 85%, a prevalence of 10%, each estimated to within 5
percentage points with 95% confidence (Buderer's method).

```{r buderer}
acc <- calc_diagnostic_accuracy(sens = 0.90, spec = 0.85, prevalence = 0.10, prec_sens = 0.05, prec_spec = 0.05, conf_level = 0.95)
c(for_sensitivity = acc$n_sens, for_specificity = acc$n_spec)
```

1383 for the sensitivity, as in the article. The study needs the larger of the two numbers.

## Better than a reference value

The appendicitis CT example of the same article: sensitivity from 90% to 95%, specificity from 80% to 85%, prevalence 40%,
two-sided 5%, 90% power.

```{r vs-reference}
ref <- calc_diagnostic_vs_reference(sens0 = 0.90, sens1 = 0.95, spec0 = 0.80, spec1 = 0.85, prevalence = 0.40,
                                    alpha = 0.05, power = 0.90, alternative = "two.sided")
c(for_sensitivity = ref$n_sens, for_specificity = ref$n_spec, needed = ref$n)
ref$binding
```

The article gives 849 and 1093; it rounds intermediate values, and the unrounded calculation here is one higher.

## Two tests in the same patients

When every patient has both tests, the number depends on how often the two tests disagree, which is rarely known in advance; the
function gives the range from the smallest to the largest possible disagreement. Akoglu's paired example, 70% against 80%,
one-sided:

```{r paired}
pr <- calc_diagnostic_two_paired(p1 = 0.70, p2 = 0.80, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80, alternative = "greater")
c(fewest = pr$n_min, most = pr$n_max)
```

The article's range is 78 to 252 (again one lower, from rounding). Two tests in different patients: `calc_diagnostic_two_indep()`.

## The area under the ROC curve

Showing that an AUC of 0.73 differs from 0.5, with 1.7 controls per case, two-sided 5%, 95% power (the S100B example of
`pROC::power.roc.test()`):

```{r roc}
roc <- calc_roc_auc(auc = 0.73, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.95, kappa = 1.7)
c(cases = roc$n_cases, controls = roc$n_controls)
```

Two AUCs, here partial AUCs over false-positive rates from 0 to 0.2 (Obuchowski & McClish 1997, Example 2, binormal parameters
A = 2.6 and 1.9, B = 1, correlation 0.6):

```{r two-aucs}
two <- calc_compare_two_aucs(A1 = 2.6, B1 = 1, A2 = 1.9, B2 = 1, rn = 0.6, ra = 0.6, delta = 0.037, alpha = 0.05, power = 0.8,
                             fpr11 = 0, fpr12 = 0.2, fpr21 = 0, fpr22 = 0.2)
c(cases = two$n_cases, controls = two$n_controls)
```

The raw value is 107.02 per group; this package always rounds up, to 108.

## Other functions

- `calc_diagnostic_ppv_npv()`: precision of the predictive values, which depend on the prevalence.
- `calc_diagnostic_likelihood_ratio()`: precision of a likelihood ratio (Simel, Samsa & Matchar 1991).
- `calc_diagnostic_odds_ratio()`: testing that the diagnostic odds ratio differs from 1.
- Agreement between two raters or two methods is in **Agreement & Reliability**: `calc_kappa()`, `calc_icc()`,
  `calc_agreement_bland_altman()`, `calc_agreement_ccc()`, `calc_agreement_cronbach()`.

Each help page gives the source of its formula and an example.
